plan:
FINAL EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN (stage = result — design deliverable only; no experiment is claimed to have been run)

Confirmed fixed requirements incorporated: U1 (primary generator = SMILES autoregressive model; graph-based generator as clearly-labeled supplementary robustness analysis), U2 (ChEMBL base/reference corpus, GuacaMol/MoleculeNet-style distribution metrics, single protein target with frozen pretrained affinity predictor), U3 (realistic compute estimates with concrete numbers, single-GPU scale), U4 (primary comparison = feedback vs. no-feedback; external property-optimization baselines as reference points only), U5 (pre-registered effect-size thresholds derived from reference-set statistics, run in parallel with distribution-level hypothesis tests), U6 (single-target affinity + multi-property joint objective; all three signals in the loop with explicit weights, iteration strategy, and ablation mapping), plus Arm G retention with explicit detection-validation criteria and a pre-specified multiplicity/no-harm statistical protocol.

=====================================================================
1. OBJECTIVES AND HYPOTHESES
=====================================================================
Primary research question (from task.json, verbatim scope): does embedding the chemical feedback loop (p-logP, QED, binding affinity) improve property scores, reduce molecular hallucination, and better align generation with real-world distributions while preserving structural diversity?

H1 (property benefit): The feedback-augmented arm produces molecules with higher penalized logP, QED, and predicted pIC50 than the no-feedback baseline under matched compute and sample budgets.
H2 (hallucination reduction): The feedback arm has a lower hallucination-composite rate than the baseline.
H3 (no-harm / fidelity–diversity preservation): The feedback arm's structural diversity and distributional fidelity are statistically equivalent (not merely "not significantly worse") to the baseline and to the real-world reference distribution — in particular, the frequency of ultra-long carbon chains does not exceed the reference-anchored threshold.

The question is inherently joint: H1–H3 must all hold for a "yes" answer. A "yes on properties / no on no-harm" outcome is reported as a partial result, not a success.

=====================================================================
2. EXPERIMENTAL ARMS: DEFINITIONS AND RATIONALE
=====================================================================
All arms share: identical pre-trained base generator (Section 3.1), identical decoding configuration (temperature, top-p, max length), identical scorer versions, identical total compute budget (gradient steps + sampled molecules), and 5 random seeds each.

• Arm A — Full feedback (primary intervention): iterative feedback loop using all three signals (Section 4). Rationale: this is the mechanism named in the question.
• Arm B — No-feedback baseline (primary comparator): same pre-trained generator, no fine-tuning, decodes the same total number of molecules as A's full pipeline (including A's intermediate feedback rounds) so that sampling budgets are matched. Rationale: isolates the effect of the feedback loop itself.
• Arm C — Ablation, p-logP only: identical loop, reward weight vector (1,0,0).
• Arm D — Ablation, QED only: weights (0,1,0).
• Arm E — Ablation, binding affinity only: weights (0,0,1).
  Rationale C–E: attribute the effect to individual signals (U6 requirement that each signal's contribution be ablation-mappable).
• Arm F — Non-iterative feedback: all three signals, but the same total fine-tuning compute applied in a single round (one large sample, one fine-tune) instead of R=5 rounds. Rationale: separates "having the feedback signal" from "iterating the loop"; A vs. F is the loop-depth ablation.
• Arm G — Degenerate pure property optimizer (negative control, retained per your instruction): aggressive optimization of p-logP + QED only (no affinity, no diversity constraint), run with a deliberately strong optimization pressure (e.g., more fine-tune rounds and top-5% retention) chosen to over-optimize. Rationale: it exists to validate that the measurement apparatus can detect the known pathology (property inflation accompanied by ultra-long-chain over-representation and scaffold collapse). Judgment criteria for G are pre-specified in Section 9.
• Optional supplementary arm (non-core, U1): Arm A′ — Arm A's loop replicated with a graph-based generator (e.g., a MoLeR-class model) at reduced seed count (3 seeds). Labeled "additional robustness analysis"; no core conclusion depends on it.

Primary contrasts: A vs. B (all three hypotheses). Secondary contrasts: A vs. C/D/E/F (attribution); B vs. reference set (baseline calibration); A vs. G (shows the feedback loop avoids the degenerate failure mode). External property-optimization baselines from the literature (e.g., published RL-optimizer results on the same benchmarks) are cited as reference points only (U4), not used for inference.

=====================================================================
3. DATA AND SCORER SPECIFICATION
=====================================================================
3.1 Corpus (U2)
• Source: ChEMBL (latest available release at execution time, e.g., ChEMBL35), small-molecule activity-annotated compounds.
• Pre-registration filter (applied identically to all uses): RDKit-parseable; heavy atoms 10–50; elements {C,H,N,O,S,F,Cl,Br,I,P}; no disallowed valences; neutralize salts (keep largest fragment); deduplicate by canonical SMILES.
• Split: (i) TRAIN (≈ 90%) for pre-training the base generator and training the affinity predictor; (ii) REFERENCE (≈ 10%, disjoint) as the "real-world distribution" anchor for all distribution metrics and threshold derivation (Section 8); REFERENCE is never used for training and is fixed before any arm runs.
3.2 Target and affinity predictor (U2, A5)
• Single target: dopamine D2 receptor (DRD2), chosen because it is the standard public-affinity benchmark in molecular generation literature with abundant ChEMBL pIC50/Ki data; any comparably annotated target may be substituted before pre-registration, after which it is fixed.
• Predictor: a frozen pretrained molecular property model (e.g., MolFormer/ChemBERTa-class encoder or an MPNN) fine-tuned once on the DRD2 affinity subset of TRAIN, then FROZEN; calibration checked on a held-out slice of TRAIN (report Spearman ρ and RMSE in the design's execution record; the predictor is never updated during the experiment).
3.3 Scorers (all frozen, identical across arms)
• Penalized logP (p-logP): standard definition — cLogP − synthetic accessibility (SA) score − ring-count penalty (0.6 × number of rings > 6), the GCPN/JT-VAE convention.
• QED: RDKit Bickerton–QED (weighted geometric mean of 8 physicochemical desirability terms).
• Binding affinity: predicted pIC50 from the frozen predictor (Section 3.2).
• Chain-length measurement: for each molecule, build the carbon-only subgraph; compute the longest simple path (number of carbon atoms) via exhaustive DFS with pruning (feasible: drug-like carbon graphs are small; a cap of 60 carbons is a safety bound). "Ultra-long" is defined relative to REFERENCE, not a fixed constant (Section 8).

=====================================================================
4. FEEDBACK LOOP SPECIFICATION (U6)
=====================================================================
4.1 Reward construction
Each generated molecule receives z-scored signals using REFERENCE-set mean/SD for p-logP and QED (z = (x − μ_ref)/σ_ref, clipped to [−3, +3]) and TRAIN-affinity-set mean/SD for pIC50. Composite reward:
  R = w_P·z(p-logP) + w_Q·z(QED) + w_A·z(pIC50), with baseline weights w = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3).
Weight rationale: equal weighting is the neutral default absent a stated priority among the three signals named in the question; a ±20% weight sensitivity analysis on Arm A is pre-registered as an exploratory check (not used for conclusions).
4.2 Iteration strategy (Arm A, C, D, E)
R = 5 rounds. Round r: (a) sample 10,000 molecules from the current policy; (b) score with the three scorers; (c) keep the top 25% by R (rejection-sampling fine-tuning, RAFT-style); (d) fine-tune the generator for a fixed number of steps (2,000 updates, constant learning rate 1e-5, AdamW). After round 5, the final policy samples the evaluation set. The loop is deliberately simple (no critic, no KL-penalty hyperparameter tuning) so that ablation arms differ only in the reward vector and round count — this maximizes interpretability of A vs. C/D/E/F contrasts.
4.3 Budget matching (control-critical)
Arms A/C/D/E/F each consume 5,000 fine-tune steps total and sample 50,000 intermediate + 20,000 evaluation molecules (A/C/D/E: 5×10k intermediate; F: 1×50k one-shot). Arm B samples 70,000 molecules with no training (10k intermediate-analogue + final 20k evaluation; intermediate molecules are logged but only used for budget matching, not evaluation). Arm G uses the same budget but top-5% retention and 2× fine-tune steps, explicitly to induce over-optimization (this is its designed purpose). All arms are compute-matched at 70k decodes; fine-tuning compute differs only where it is the manipulated variable (G), and that difference is itself part of G's definition.

=====================================================================
5. METRICS: DEFINITIONS AND COMPUTATION DETAILS
=====================================================================
5.1 Property metrics (H1): mean/median p-logP, QED, predicted pIC50 over valid unique molecules; also the composite score R̄ (evaluation-time scoring, using the same z-scoring as Section 4.1). Primary endpoint (pre-registered, single): mean composite property score on the evaluation set. Secondary: the three individual property metrics.
5.2 Standard generation metrics: validity rate (RDKit-parsable), uniqueness rate (unique canonical SMILES / valid), novelty (fraction of unique valid molecules absent from TRAIN ∪ REFERENCE).
5.3 Hallucination composite (H2), pre-registered as the unweighted mean of four rates:
  (a) invalid rate (1 − validity);
  (b) chemically implausible rate: SA score > 6 or RDKit valence/fragment warnings;
  (c) out-of-distribution rate: maximum Tanimoto similarity (2048-bit Morgan, radius 2) to any REFERENCE molecule below the REFERENCE 1st-percentile NN-similarity value (threshold computed from REFERENCE, pre-registered as a rule);
  (d) structural-artifact rate: longest carbon chain ≥ REFERENCE 95th percentile (the named failure mode; counted once here and reported in detail under 5.4).
5.4 Structural diversity and fidelity (H3):
  (i) Chain-length distribution: histogram of longest-carbon-chain length (bins = integers 1..P95_ref..max), compared against REFERENCE by χ² (pooled small bins ≥5 counts) and by the ultra-long-chain rate (fraction ≥ P95_ref).
  (ii) Scaffold diversity: unique Bemis–Murcko scaffold ratio; scaffold classes count normalized by N.
  (iii) Internal diversity: mean nearest-neighbor Tanimoto similarity within the arm (lower = more diverse).
  (iv) Physicochemical fidelity: KS statistics between arm and REFERENCE for MW, cLogP, TPSA, HBD, HBA, ring count.
5.5 Implementation: all metrics computed with RDKit + GuacaMol-style utilities; all evaluation code frozen and run once per (arm, seed) sample; no post-hoc metric selection.

=====================================================================
6. CONTROLS
=====================================================================
1. Identical base generator and initialization shared by all arms (single pre-training run; not retrained per arm).
2. Identical decoding parameters (temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, max length 128 tokens) and identical evaluation sample size per arm–seed.
3. Five seeds per core arm (A–G); seed treated as a random effect; every reported statistic is the mean over seed-level estimates ± across-seed SD.
4. Frozen scorers and frozen predictor across all arms (Section 3.2–3.3); scorer versions and checksums logged.
5. Identical post-processing: none beyond RDKit parse — invalid molecules are counted, not silently filtered (filtering would bias validity comparison).
6. Budget matching (Section 4.3) so that A vs. B differs only in the presence/iteration of feedback.
7. Pre-registration: all metrics, thresholds, tests, and correction method (Section 8) fixed in this document before any generation; evaluation code written to read this specification literally.

=====================================================================
7. SAMPLE SIZE AND COMPUTE ESTIMATE (U3 — concrete, single-GPU scale)
=====================================================================
• Evaluation sample: N = 20,000 valid-unique-target molecules per arm–seed (GuacaMol-benchmark convention), 5 seeds → 100,000 evaluated molecules per arm; 7 core arms → 700,000 evaluated decodes total.
• Power justification (rule-based, not invented): with N = 20,000 per arm and 5 seeds, a between-arm standardized difference of 0.1 SD is detectable at >99% power (two-sided α=0.05); the effect thresholds in Section 8 are ≥0.25 SD, hence generously powered. N=20,000 is adopted because it is the community-standard benchmark sample size, which also makes results comparable to published reference baselines (U4).
• Compute estimate (NVIDIA A100-80GB class, realistic "affordable" framing, not unlimited):
  – Base SMILES generator: ~35M-parameter transformer (8 layers, d=512), pre-trained once on TRAIN (~2M ChEMBL SMILES, 3 epochs): ≈ 10 GPU-hours (one-time, shared by all arms).
  – Affinity predictor training (one-time, then frozen): ≈ 2 GPU-hours.
  – Per trained arm (A, C, D, E, F, G): 5,000 fine-tune steps + 50k intermediate + 20k evaluation decodes ≈ 2–3 GPU-hours each → ≈ 15 GPU-hours for 6 trained arms.
  – Arm B: decoding only, ≈ 0.5 GPU-hour.
  – Scoring all molecules (RDKit metrics + affinity prediction on ~1.4M molecules including intermediates): ≈ 3–4 GPU-hours.
  – Supplementary graph-generator arm A′: ≈ 8 GPU-hours.
  Total ≈ 40–50 GPU-hours core + ≈ 8 GPU-hours supplementary — i.e., ~3–4 A100-days, or ~1 week on a single shared GPU. CPU-only fallback: generation/fine-tuning is not feasible on CPU, but all metric computation is; this does not affect the design-only deliverable.

=====================================================================
8. STATISTICAL ANALYSIS AND PRE-REGISTERED CRITERIA (U5)
=====================================================================
8.1 Threshold derivation rule (general principle): every threshold is a function of REFERENCE-set statistics computed once, before arm comparison, and written into the analysis script; no threshold is chosen after seeing arm results. Where absolute numbers are quoted below (e.g., "QED SD ≈ 0.2"), they are literature-typical ChEMBL values used only for power illustration; the binding values are the rules "0.25 × σ_ref", "P95_ref", etc., evaluated on the actual REFERENCE set at analysis time.
8.2 Property superiority (H1): success requires the primary endpoint (mean composite score) to improve over Arm B by Δ ≥ 0.25 × σ_ref(composite) (i.e., at least a quarter of the reference-set standard deviation — a deliberately conservative small-effect floor) with a Holm-corrected p < 0.05 (Mann–Whitney U on pooled molecules, with a seed-level permutation check as robustness). Secondary individual-metric thresholds (all anchored to 0.25 × σ_ref of the corresponding REFERENCE statistic): ΔQED ≥ 0.25·σ_QED,ref (illustratively ≈ +0.05 if σ_QED ≈ 0.2), Δp-logP ≥ 0.25·σ_plogP,ref, ΔpIC50 ≥ 0.25·σ_pIC50,ref (illustratively ≈ +0.4–0.5 log units if σ ≈ 1.6–2.0; note 0.5 log units = 3.2× activity, a conventional meaningful potency change).
8.3 No-harm criteria (H3) — equivalence testing, not absence-of-significance: each criterion is tested with two one-sided tests (TOST) at α = 0.05 against pre-registered margins:
  (a) Unique-scaffold ratio: relative drop vs. Arm B ≤ 5% (margin justified by the bootstrap 95% CI width of the REFERENCE scaffold ratio, which is ≲2–3% at N=100k; the margin is ~2× that sampling noise floor);
  (b) Mean internal NN-Tanimoto: increase vs. Arm B ≤ 0.05 absolute (≈ 0.25 × typical within-ChEMBL NN-similarity SD);
  (c) Chain-length distribution: KS statistic vs. REFERENCE ≤ 0.10 (small-effect convention for distribution distance);
  (d) Ultra-long-chain rate: ≤ 1.5 × REFERENCE rate AND ≤ REFERENCE rate + 2 percentage points (P95 anchoring guarantees the baseline rate is ~5%; the 1.5×/2-pp margins are ~2–3× the bootstrap sampling noise of that rate at N=100k);
  (e) Physicochemical fidelity: per-property KS vs. REFERENCE ≤ 0.10 for all six properties in 5.4(iv).
8.4 Hallucination (H2): rate ratio (A/B) with 95% CI; success if upper CI bound < 1 (i.e., significant reduction) with no individual composite component worsening beyond its Section 8.3 margin.
8.5 Multiple-comparison correction (pre-specified, no post-hoc metric picking): two pre-declared families —
  Family 1 (primary, 1 test): A vs. B on the composite endpoint (Holm correction trivially applies within family);
  Family 2 (secondary, fixed and enumerated): A vs. B on {p-logP, QED, pIC50, hallucination composite, ultra-long rate, scaffold ratio, NN-Tanimoto} = 7 tests → Holm–Bonferroni within Family 2;
  Family 3 (attribution, exploratory): A vs. C/D/E/F and weight-sensitivity tests (10 tests) → Holm within Family 3; results labeled exploratory, never load-bearing.
  Hierarchical gating: the overall question is answered "yes" only if Family 1 passes, all Family-2 no-harm criteria pass TOST, and H2 passes; otherwise the specific failure is named.
8.6 Distribution-level tests run in parallel with the thresholds (U5): χ² on chain-length bins (arm vs. REFERENCE and arm vs. B), KS tests on physicochemical properties, all at α = 0.05 with Holm correction inside their own subfamily; these complement, and never replace, the effect-size thresholds.

=====================================================================
9. ARM G: DETECTION-VALIDATION CRITERIA (negative control, explicit)
=====================================================================
G is a methodological control, not a competitor. Pre-specified pass criteria (all three must hold; if any fails, the measurement apparatus is declared insufficiently sensitive and the design's operationalizations must be revised before any interpretive claim):
  G1: G's mean p-logP and QED exceed Arm B's by ≥ 0.5 × σ_ref each (proving the optimizer genuinely moves properties);
  G2: G's ultra-long-chain rate ≥ 2 × REFERENCE rate and TOST-equivalence to REFERENCE fails on the KS ≤ 0.10 margin (proving chain-length pathology is detectable);
  G3: G's unique-scaffold ratio drops ≥ 15% relative to Arm B (proving scaffold collapse is detectable).
Only after G validates the apparatus do A-vs-B conclusions carry weight; this ordering is part of the analysis plan.

=====================================================================
10. FEASIBILITY
=====================================================================
All components are open-source and standard: RDKit (validity, QED, SA, cLogP, scaffolds, Tanimoto), GuacaMol-style distribution metrics, public ChEMBL data, a public DRD2 affinity subset, and an open pretrained affinity model or a small from-scratch MPNN. The loop uses rejection-sampling fine-tuning, the simplest RL-free feedback instantiation, minimizing implementation risk and keeping ablations clean. The current workspace (no RDKit/torch, network disabled) is consistent with design-only delivery per track.md; execution would occur in an environment with network access for ChEMBL download and package installation. No wet-lab component exists; binding affinity is predicted, not measured (A5, U2) — a stated limitation.

=====================================================================
11. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITATIONS (explicit list)
=====================================================================
Assumptions (design rests on these; each was flagged in the plan stage and either confirmed by you or retained as a reasonable default):
  A1. "Chemical feedback mechanism" = iterative generate→score→select→fine-tune loop over the three named signals (implementation class not specified by the task; RAFT-style chosen for interpretability).
  A2. Baseline = identical pre-trained generator without feedback (U4-confirmed as the primary comparison).
  A3. "Molecular hallucination" = the four-component composite of Section 5.3 (invalid, implausible, OOD, structural artifact).
  A4. "Ultra-long carbon chain" = longest carbon-chain length ≥ REFERENCE 95th percentile (reference-anchored, not a fixed constant).
  A5. Binding affinity = frozen pretrained in-silico predictor on DRD2 (confirmed, U2).
  A6. DRD2 is an acceptable stand-in for "targeted molecule discovery" — substitutable before pre-registration, fixed thereafter.
  A7. Equal reward weights (1/3 each) are a neutral default; sensitivity analysis covers this but cannot rule out that a different weighting changes conclusions.
  A8. One generator architecture (SMILES autoregressive) suffices for the core conclusion (U1-confirmed); the graph-model check is supplementary only.
Limitations:
  L1. Predicted, not experimental, affinity: conclusions are about the feedback loop's effect on scores and distributions, not about real biological activity.
  L2. Single target and single corpus: generalization to other targets/assays is untested within this design (supplementary A′ tests architecture robustness only).
  L3. The hallucination composite is one operationalization; other definitions (e.g., retrosynthetic-feasibility models) could yield different answers; the composite is fixed in advance to prevent post-hoc selection, but its face validity is a judgment call.
  L4. Chain-length thresholds anchored to ChEMBL's distribution inherit any biases in that corpus (e.g., enumerators' length preferences); results are "aligned with ChEMBL-like real-world distributions," not with chemical space at large.
  L5. Equal-budget matching constrains what "feedback benefit" means: it measures benefit per unit of compute, not the attainable optimum with unlimited tuning.
  L6. RAFT-style feedback is one point in the space of feedback algorithms; a stronger RL method might show larger gains or different diversity behavior — the design answers the question for this mechanism class, and this scope is stated, not hidden.
  L7. All numeric SDs quoted for power illustration are literature-typical values pending actual REFERENCE computation; only the rules (0.25σ_ref, P95_ref, TOST margins) are binding.

END OF DESIGN DELIVERABLE. This document specifies an experiment; nothing herein asserts that any arm, generation run, or analysis has been executed.

context.question: Incorporating the chemical feedback mechanism, which leverages properties such as p-logP, QED, and binding affinity, directly improves the generation of molecules with superior chemical properties and reduces molecular hallucinations in targeted molecule discovery tasks. Does embedding this feedback loop better align molecule generation with real-world distributions, preserving structural diversity (e.g., avoiding over-representation of ultra-long carbon chains) while enhancing property scores?
context.context: Design an experiment that answers the question. The researcher can clarify source-supported setup details by topic. Do not claim that an experiment was run.
